html:
The Battle of Valmy was fought on 20 September 1792 near the village of Valmy in Champagne, northeastern France. A French army under Generals Dumouriez and Kellermann stopped a Prussian army under the Duke of Brunswick that was marching on Paris.

Three years into the French Revolution, France went to war with Austria, and Prussia joined in. Brunswick threatened to destroy Paris if the royal family was harmed. His army took the forts of Longwy and Verdun. At Valmy about 36,000 French, a mix of old regular soldiers and new volunteers, stood on a ridge. The battle was mostly a duel of cannon. The Prussian infantry advanced, saw that the French did not run, and was called back. Each side lost only a few hundred men. Ten days later the Prussians, sick and short of food, began to retreat.

The revolution was saved. The next day a new assembly in Paris ended the monarchy, and France became a republic. Valmy was the first big victory of the French Revolutionary Wars, which were fought by mass citizen armies. The German writer Goethe, who was with the Prussians, later wrote that a new era in world history began there that day.
